title: Meropenem
sources: Roberts JA, et al. DALI study — defining antibiotic levels in intensive care unit patients. Clin Infect Dis. 2014;58(8):1072-1083.

Standard renal dose-reduction table (eGFR-tiered) as commonly summarized in critical-care pharmacy references; confirm precise cutoffs against your institution's renal dosing protocol and current product labeling.

changelog.change: Initial entry — a genuine content gap, second card in the new Antimicrobial Dosing category.

mechanism: Broad-spectrum carbapenem — covers most gram-negatives (including many ESBL producers and Pseudomonas), gram-positives, and anaerobes. Like other beta-lactams, killing is time-dependent (time above MIC), so extended infusion improves target attainment the same way it does for piperacillin-tazobactam.
onset: Within the first infusion; extended/continuous infusion improves sustained exposure more than peak effect.
duration: Redosed every 8 h at standard renal function; interval widens as renal function falls.
dosing:
Standard (normal renal function): 1 g IV q8h. Use 2 g q8h for CNS infection, severe Pseudomonas infection, or other indications needing higher CNS/tissue penetration.
Extended-infusion strategy (preferred in critical illness/sepsis): infuse the dose over 3 hours rather than the traditional 30 minutes, for the same PK/PD rationale as piperacillin-tazobactam.
Renal dose reduction (typical eGFR tiers — confirm against your institution's protocol, as exact cutoffs vary by source): eGFR > 50 mL/min — no change; eGFR 25-50 — 1 g q12h; eGFR < 25 — 0.5 g q12h; eGFR < 10 / dialysis — 0.5 g q24h, with supplemental post-dialysis dosing on hemodialysis days.
cautions: CI: known carbapenem anaphylaxis. Cross-reactivity with penicillin allergy is real but lower than once assumed — a history of penicillin allergy is not an automatic carbapenem contraindication, but confirm your institution's approach for severe/anaphylactic penicillin reactions.

AEs: seizures — a class effect of carbapenems, meropenem carries a lower risk than imipenem but it is not zero, and risk rises sharply with inadequate renal dose reduction, pre-existing CNS disease, or very high doses. This is the single most important reason NOT to skip the renal adjustment.

Precautions: reduces valproic acid levels significantly (a well-described interaction) — avoid co-administration where possible, or monitor levels closely and expect breakthrough seizures if a patient is on valproate for seizure control.
pearls: The valproate interaction is easy to miss and can precipitate status epilepticus in a patient previously well-controlled — actively check the med list before starting meropenem in anyone on valproic acid.

Meropenem is often reached for specifically for its CNS penetration and Pseudomonas coverage together — if neither is needed, a narrower or non-carbapenem agent is frequently more appropriate stewardship.
